# Incident Postmortem: Connection Pool Exhaustion (4h Outage)

**Date:** 2026-10-12  
**Severity:** SEV-1 | **Duration:** 4h 23m  
**Affected:** API service, 100% traffic | **Peak impact:** 50K failed requests

---

## Timeline

| Time | Event |
|------|-------|
| 14:32 | Payment service latency spike (p99 20s → 180s) detected; alerts silent |
| 14:47 | Downstream payment provider experiencing capacity issues; slow responses backlog |
| 15:08 | Connection pool exhausted (128 → 0 available); requests queue indefinitely |
| 15:11 | Alerts fire (error rate 95%+); on-call paged |
| 15:15 | Incident lead starts; identifies pool exhaustion via metrics dashboard |
| 15:22 | Root cause: payment service returning bodies slowly; connections held open waiting |
| 15:31 | Mitigation #1: reduced pool wait timeout from 30s → 5s; errors instead of hangs |
| 15:43 | Partial recovery; ~40% traffic succeeds; circuit breaker engaged for payment calls |
| 16:14 | Downstream provider recovers; latency returns to baseline (200ms) |
| 16:29 | Full recovery; monitoring confirms all metrics nominal |
| 18:55 | Postmortem window closed |

---

## Root Cause

**Payment service returned to normal response time (200ms) but *streamed* response bodies slowly (8–15s), holding HTTP connections open.** Our service waited for full body receipt before returning the connection to the pool. 128-pool capacity exhausted in ~90s.

**Why alerts didn't fire:** latency alerts monitored *request start-to-response header* (fast); connection pool depth had no alert.

---

## Contributing Factors

1. **No pool depth visibility.** Metric missing from dashboard; exhaustion went 15min unnoticed.
2. **No read timeout on HTTP client.** Slow body streaming = connection held until client-side timeout (never configured).
3. **No circuit breaker on payment calls.** Dependent slow → all requests blocked, no failover.
4. **Synchronous, unbounded retry.** Failed calls retried immediately, re-queued against empty pool.

---

## Remediations

### Immediate (done 16:45)
- **Circuit breaker on payment API:** fail open after 3 consecutive timeouts or 50% error rate (5min window). [[PR#8421](https://github.com/internal/api/pull/8421)]
- **HTTP client read timeout:** 10s (payment SLA + margin).
- **Connection pool metrics:** `pool.available`, `pool.queued` → Grafana dashboard. Alarm at <10 available.

### Short-term (48h)
- **Exponential backoff on retries:** max 3, jitter 100–5000ms. [[PR#8433](https://github.com/internal/api/pull/8433)]
- **Graceful degradation:** payment calls timeout → return cached order status (read-only). [[Ticket ENG-4421](https://linear.com/issue/ENG-4421)]

### Long-term (sprint planning)
- **Async payment confirmation:** decouple request-response from status updates; webhooks instead. [[Proposal RFC-0087](https://wiki.internal/rfc-0087)]
- **Pool auto-scaling:** monitor queue depth; scale up on sustained pressure (1s+ wait times). {{Estimate: 8pts}}
- **Dependency SLA monitoring:** per-endpoint baselines; auto-alert on drift >2σ.

---

## Prevention

- Alerting on pool depth is non-negotiable for any external dependency.
- HTTP timeouts (connect, read, total) must be explicit; timeouts ≤ SLA.
- Synchronous blocking calls to external services require circuit breakers or queue-based isolation.
- Load tests should include slow-body scenarios (chunked encoding, gradual payloads).

---

## Action Items

| Owner | Item | Due | Priority |
|-------|------|-----|----------|
| @payments-team | Circuit breaker tuning (test with prod traffic shadow mode) | Oct 14 | P0 |
| @platform | Pool monitoring alert → on-call runbook | Oct 13 | P0 |
| @infrastructure | Dependency SLA baseline tooling | Oct 20 | P1 |
| @qa | Slow-body load test suite | Oct 27 | P2 |

---

## Lessons

**Connections are a resource pool like memory or goroutines. Invisible pools don't get managed; invisible pools exhaust under load.** Slow *downstream* behavior (not slowness *detecting* it) was the surprise — response headers fast, but body-read hung callers. Read timeouts matter more than latency alarms for I/O-bound systems.
